Sleep medicine · published research

Sleep quality

A 2026 meta-analysis of five trials found a modest improvement in PSQI scores versus sham. A newer 40-person transcranial trial reported lower insomnia severity, sleep disturbances, and sleep latency. Other studies show mixed objective or between-group outcomes.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A 2026 meta-analysis of five trials found a modest improvement in PSQI scores versus sham. A newer 40-person transcranial trial reported lower insomnia severity, sleep disturbances, and sleep latency. Other studies show mixed objective or between-group outcomes.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Sleep medicine > Sleep quality category contains 15 titles: 13 human reports, one meta-analysis, and one narrative review. Ten human reports are randomized trials; the rest are single-arm, retrospective, or observational studies. A translational paper includes a human randomized trial plus mouse and cell experiments, so those methods do not represent separate publications. The 2026 meta-analysis searched studies through September 2025 and does not include the newer translational report.

Human and clinical evidence

The 2026 meta-analysis pooled five randomized trials with 240 participants and found a modest PSQI improvement versus sham, with a mean difference of -1.25 points and a wide confidence interval from -2.38 to -0.11 (de Azevedo et al. 2026). A later 40-person double-blind trial of transcranial PBM reported lower insomnia severity, fewer sleep disturbances, and shorter sleep latency (Jung et al. 2026). Other small trials include a sham-controlled device study and trials in people with cognitive complaints, nurses, or older adults. A wearable study in people with depression improved PSQI scores without a between-group depression benefit (Guu et al. 2025). Populations and measures vary, and actigraphy, melatonin, and other objective outcomes are not uniformly positive.

Animal evidence

The translational report found increased non-REM sleep and frontal delta power in mice after transcranial near-infrared exposure. This is mechanistic evidence, not proof of patient benefit.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

The same translational paper includes a cell experiment related to adenosine signaling. It is one publication's laboratory arm, not a separate sleep trial.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Studies use transcranial light, wearable near-infrared devices, body exposure, and laser acupuncture, with different wavelengths and schedules. Wavelength is the light's color band and affects how far it may travel through tissue. A PSQI score, insomnia severity, actigraphy, and melatonin measure different aspects of sleep and should not be treated as interchangeable.

Interpretation

Subjective sleep scores show a modest pooled signal, with a newer small trial reporting additional positive outcomes. Protocol and population differences, limited precision, and mixed objective findings leave durability and broad clinical use uncertain.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term subjective sleep improvement with some transcranial or wearable protocols Low for objective sleep measures, durability, or generalization across sleep disorders
Publications and records15 unique titles (exact Sleep medicine > Sleep quality)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A 2026 meta-analysis of five randomized trials found a modest PSQI improvement with limited precision, and a newer translational trial reported better insomnia scores. Other trials vary in device, population, and outcome, with objective measures often mixed. Independent studies should assess sleep objectively and follow outcomes after treatment ends.
